Gender could be called fluid, only insofar as it is not a fixed physical phenomenon and undergoes modification throughout a lifetime. It is more accurate to say that gender is plastic for everyone to different degrees. If you are immediately offended by this, it's likely that your understanding of gender fluidity is given to you by the Left, who have perverted the concept to fit their own ideology. Their fundamental error is to assume bi-directionality in the information flow from material world to psychological world. Fluid means an ability to flow easily and yield easily to external pressures due to an unfixed shape. As we'll see, gender does yield in abstract ways to external social cues, but it is NOT fluid in the sense that it changes with every jostle of the container, or that it could become radically different in relatively short periods of time, say if you metaphorically spilled the jar.

Rather, it is plastic, in the sense that over a lifetime it is something malleable, which is molded by a multitude of factors, not the least of which IS your biological sex. Gender is a psychological experience that descends through life with modifications as you are socialized and you learn what society expects from you.

Sex is the physical state of your chromosomes, and assuming normal development, also the state of your genitals.

Gender, is a psychological construct. It is your own self-concept of yourself as that sex, and it is informed by several things:

(1) your sex

(2) your parents and your exposure to them in infancy

(3) your social development including with your siblings and your peer group as you age

(4) your own self-perceived social status at any and any point after you develop awareness of it

Notice that gender is informed by both social factors and innate biological factors, because gender is not a concrete material thing, but a changing subjective phenomenon. I'd define it as the subjective experience of your sex within a society which has evolved real expectations about your sexual behavior.

You have a stomach. That stomach can be empty. But the experience of hunger is neither that stomach, nor its emptiness. It is a phenomenon separate, but still coupled, to those things.

For example, even if at age 10 you recognized yourself as the male sex, your self-concept of how masculine you are is going to be different than your masculine self-concept at age 35. When you are 35 you will (likely) feel more masculine in your self-perception, because you'll feel more in adherence to gender roles and biological expectations from a society which has been imprinting these on you for your entire life (i.e. chest hair, larger body mass, muscles, physicality and your work capacity). Yet, your chromosomes did not change. But something did. This is important. When we say gender changes, or is plastic, the mistake is to think it is binary. It isn't "on" or "off". In the example I provided just above, your gender was never not in the quadrants of male. But you proceeded further along the plot to an actualized masculine nature on the journey from age 10 to age 35. Your own psychological perception of yourself as a man evolved.

This is over-simplifying the picture. Because the plasticity of gender is psychological, but it can be effected by physiology. For example, part of the process of your changing view of your manhood in that example was puberty, and the male sex hormones have tangible effects on the brain, which effects the psychology.

Here is where liberals get it wrong. Sex (biology) can inform gender, but GENDER CANNOT INFORM SEX. Meaning no matter what, you are never not the biological sex you were born. A psychological construct does not change physical reality, but it can be informed by those physical realities. In other words, gender dysphoria is an abnormal psychological condition, and it can be changed with psychological treatment. Another mistake is to assume that fluidity means as a male, your gender could be healthy and be anywhere on the map. That isn't the case. In a normal psychology, we'd expect gender to track with sex. But as an example, there are plenty of examples of effeminate men out there, who are acutely aware of their nature and its normative differences from the stereotypes. Their own self-concept of their masculinity wouldn't look the same as a more masculine member of their peer group, again, because one of the major aspects informing gender is your own self-perception of your adherence to society's expectations.

If as an adult man today, you had your dick chopped off, your feelings about your masculinity would change. Your sex didn't change, right? But your self-concept did.

Note that one of the takeaways of this is that it isn't normal for a sexual male to exhibit a female gender experience (an effeminate male is still not a female-gendered male), rather it is abnormal. These understandings all came about largely from the field of abnormal psychology. Instead, think of the experience of maleness (gender) as something which varies for men on a spectrum of masculinity and femininity. It is the same with the female gender, as opposed to the female sex. Problems arise in the Leftist ideologies when males identify as females, for example. A healthy male could lean toward an effeminate nature, while still being cognizant of and accepting his male sex.

But even if we take the example of a highly effeminate male in a society with discrete sexual roles, we can see how there could be social stresses for that person. The male child who grows up with an affinity for art and poetry versus the more normative expectation of the male child who plays sports. A lot of the difficulty of our teenage years is directly tied to the plasticity of gender, the shaping of our self image according to the social and biological cues of sex. That's why perhaps the most important perspectives on these ideas is toward their USEFULNESS in therapeutic interventions. In discussing psychological issues with a person who is experiencing social troubles related to behavior, if all we could do to define terms about their experience amounted to "man" and "woman", we couldn't get very far. Being able to refer concretely to subjective concepts which aren't concrete gives us the ability to recognize, apprehend, judge, and adjust behavior. Therefore, gender is a model. A linguistic/psychological model to approximate a spectrum of subjective experiences and the associated consequences.
